question: What position does the nurse hold in the medication safety chain?

options.A: The final safety barrier before drug entry
options.B: The legal owner of the hospital prescription pad
options.C: The primary creator of the pharmacological agent
options.D: The secondary supervisor of pharmacy inventory

explanation: Nurses check medications right before administration, making them the last defense against medication errors. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h1)

question: How should a nurse view a doctor's prescription order?

options.A: As a suggestion that can be altered freely
options.B: As a document solely meant for pharmacy records
options.C: As an order requiring independent safety verification
options.D: As a command to execute without question

explanation: Nurses must evaluate prescriptions for safety and appropriateness before giving any drug to a patient. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h1)

question: How many unique identifiers must a nurse check to confirm the right patient?
explanation: Checking at least two unique identifiers like name and hospital number prevents patient misidentification. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h2)

question: When is the correct time to record a medication in the chart?

options.A: Before pulling the medication from the trolley
options.B: At the end of the entire nursing shift
options.C: Whenever the prescribing doctor requests it

explanation: Charting must happen right after delivery to prevent accidental double-dosing or missed documentation. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h2)

question: Why must a nurse check vital signs before giving certain medications?

options.A: To fulfill mandatory hospital paperwork requirements
options.B: To establish a baseline and prevent adverse reactions
options.C: To determine the financial cost of the hospital stay
options.D: To decide which nurse is assigned to the ward

explanation: Assessing vital signs ensures the patient's body can safely handle the physiological effects of the drug. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h3)

question: Which screening action is critical before administering any new pharmaceutical agent?

options.A: Inspecting the patient's home electricity supply
options.C: Measuring the patient's exact daily fluid intake

explanation: Screening for allergies prevents severe immune responses such as anaphylactic shock. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h3)

question: What tool should a nurse use to measure liquid oral medications accurately?

options.A: A calibrated oral syringe or medicine cup

explanation: Household spoons vary greatly in size and lead to inaccurate dosing, requiring medical-grade measuring devices. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h4)

question: What is the primary danger of leaving prepared medications unattended on a tray?

options.A: Rapid evaporation of active chemical compounds
options.B: Loss of the hospital tray due to routine theft
options.C: Unwanted chemical reactions with room air temperature
options.D: Risk of contamination or incorrect patient administration

explanation: Unattended medications can be misplaced, tampered with, or given to the wrong person. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h4)

question: Why must a patient be sitting upright when taking oral medications?

options.A: To comply with traditional hospital dining rules
options.B: To make it easier for the nurse to count pills
options.C: To prevent the risk of aspiration into the lungs
options.D: To accelerate the mechanical digestion of the pill

explanation: An upright posture uses gravity to direct pills safely down the esophagus rather than the airway. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h5)

question: Which site is generally recommended as safest for intramuscular injections in adults?
explanation: The ventrogluteal site lacks major nerves and blood vessels, making it the safest location for IM injections. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h5)

question: Why is post-administration monitoring an essential part of drug administration?

options.A: To test the patient's memory regarding drug names
options.B: To complete mandatory hospital billing forms for pharmacy stock
options.C: To prove to the doctor that the nurse was present
options.D: To evaluate therapeutic effectiveness and catch adverse reactions early

explanation: Monitoring ensures the drug is working as intended and allows rapid intervention if side effects occur. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h6)

question: Which factor must be documented immediately alongside the drug name and dose?

options.A: The manufacturer of the syringe used
options.C: The cost of the pharmaceutical drug
options.D: The weather outside the hospital ward

explanation: Recording the exact time prevents dosing errors and maintains a clear timeline of care. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h6)

question: What is the very first action a nurse must take after discovering a medication error?

options.A: Complete a detailed written incident report form
options.B: Inform the hospital director of nursing immediately
options.C: Assess the patient's clinical condition and vital signs
options.D: Hide the medication packaging in a secure drawer

explanation: Patient safety and immediate physiological assessment always come first when a medication error happens. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of filing an incident report after an error?

options.A: To identify systemic workflow issues and prevent future occurrences
options.B: To provide concrete evidence for police criminal investigations
options.C: To lower the financial liability of the insurance company
options.D: To determine which staff member should be fired

explanation: Incident reports help hospitals analyze root causes and improve safety systems rather than just punishing staff. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h7)

question: Which body legally regulates nursing practice and drug administration standards in Nigeria?

options.C: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria sets the legal scope of practice and professional standards for nurses. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h8)

question: What does the ethical principle of non-maleficence mean in pharmacology?

options.A: Doing no harm to the patient through careless drug administration
options.B: Ensuring hospital pharmacies make a profit on drugs
options.C: Giving free medication to every patient in need
options.D: Allowing patients to choose any medication they want

explanation: Non-maleficence requires nurses to take every precaution to prevent injury or harm to patients. [learn more](GNS125_U4_T5#GNS125_U4_T5_h8)
